steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a paper that benchmarks surrogate-based optimisation algorithms on expensive black-box problems from real-life applications. It should explain why such a benchmark is needed and list our contributions and main findings.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Surrogate-based optimisation for expensive objectives; application areas
- Why benchmarking surrogate algorithms is hard
- Gap: no standard benchmark of real-life expensive problems
- This work: comparison + public benchmark library; list of contributions
- Extra result (continuous vs discrete models) and main insights

  - main reason: no standard benchmark set of real-life problems that also have expensive objectives
  - so hard to decide beforehand which surrogate algorithm to use on a real-life application

  - other contributions:

    3. performance vs available computational resources and cost of the objective
    4. separate effect of surrogate model choice from acquisition step
    5. easy to interpret rules of thumb: which surrogate algorithm when

  - important: variable types (continuous, integer, categorical, etc.) often used in practice to choose/discard surrogate model

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Surrogate-based optimisation algorithms, for example Bayesian optimisation, are different from other black-box optimisation algorithms because they are designed specifically for problems where the objective function is expensive. There are examples of this in materials science, temperature control, building design, aerodynamics, optics and computer vision.

These algorithms use a surrogate model that approximates the objective function, and because of that they get good results even with only a low number of function evaluations. steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Surrogate-based optimisation algorithms, for example Bayesian optimisation, are different from other black-box optimisation algorithms because they are designed specifically for problems where the objective function is expensive. There are examples of this in materials science, temperature control, building design, aerodynamics, optics and computer vision.

These algorithms use a surrogate model that approximates the objective function, and because of that they get good results even with only a low number of function evaluations. But training and using the surrogate model takes more computation than the typical black-box optimisation heuristics, like local search or population-based methods. This makes it complicated to benchmark surrogate algorithms thoroughly.

The way surrogate algorithms are benchmarked now does not give complete insight into what the different algorithms are strong and weak at, for example how computationally efficient they are or how accurate they are for different types of problems. The most important reason for this is that there is no standard benchmark set of problems that come from real-life applications and that also have expensive objective functions. Because of this it is difficult to know beforehand which surrogate algorithm to use on a real-life application.

In this work we compare several surrogate algorithms on the same set of expensive optimisation problems that come from real-life applications. This results in a public benchmark library that can easily be extended with new surrogate algorithms and also with new problems. Our other contributions are:

- 1. creating a meta-algorithmic dataset of how surrogate algorithms perform on real-life expensive problems,

- 2. insight into the strengths and weaknesses of existing surrogate algorithms depending on the properties of the problem, and checking existing knowledge from the literature,

- 3. looking at how the performance of the algorithms depends on the computational resources that are available and on the cost of the expensive objective,

- 4. separating the effect of choosing the surrogate model from the effect of the acquisition step of the different algorithms,

- 5. rules of thumb that are easy to interpret, for when to use which surrogate algorithm.

We also show that continuous models can be used on discrete problems, and the other way around. This is an important result, because in practice the types of the variables in a problem (e.g. continuous, integer, categorical, etc.) are often used to decide which surrogate model to choose or to discard. The main insights we got are that the accuracy of the surrogate model and the choice between a continuous or a discrete model are less important than the evaluation time of the objective and the way that the surrogate algorithm explores the search space.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Unlike other black-box optimisation algorithms, surrogate-based optimisation algorithms such as Bayesian optimisation [1] are designed specifically for problems with expensive objective functions. Examples can be found in materials science [2], temperature control [3], building design [4], aerodynamics [5], optics [6], and computer vision [7].

By using a surrogate model that approximates the objective function, these algorithms achieve good results even with a low number of function evaluations. However, training and using the surrogate model is more computationally intensive than using typical black-box optimisation heuristics such as local search or population-based methods. This complicates thorough benchmarking of surrogate algorithms.

The current way of benchmarking surrogate algorithms does not give complete insight into the strengths and weaknesses of the different algorithms, such as their computational efficiency or their accuracy for different types of problems. The most important reason for this is the lack of a standard benchmark set of problems that come from real-life applications and also have expensive objective functions. This makes it difficult to determine beforehand which surrogate algorithm to use on a real-life application.

In this work, we compare several surrogate algorithms on the same set of expensive optimisation problems from real-life applications, which results in a public benchmark library that can easily be extended with new surrogate algorithms as well as with new problems. Our other contributions are:

- 1. the creation of a meta-algorithmic dataset of surrogate algorithm performance on real-life expensive problems,

- 2. insight into the strengths and weaknesses of existing surrogate algorithms depending on problem properties, and verification of existing knowledge from literature,

- 3. an investigation of how algorithm performance depends on the available computational resources and the cost of the expensive objective,

- 4. separating the effects of the choice of surrogate model and of the acquisition step of the different algorithms,

- 5. easy to interpret rules of thumb for when to use which surrogate algorithm.

Furthermore, we show that continuous models can be used on discrete problems and vice versa. This is an important result, since in practice the types of variables in a problem (e.g. continuous, integer, categorical, etc.) are often used to decide which surrogate model to choose or discard. The main insights we obtained are that the accuracy of a surrogate model and the choice between a continuous or discrete model are less important than the evaluation time of the objective and the way the surrogate algorithm explores the search space.
